stages.title: Minimum and maximum wages
stages.sub: After this the student can explain how minimum and maximum wages distort the labour market and evaluate their effects.

steps.q: Workers currently paid £6 an hour are told that, by law, nobody may be paid less than £8 an hour. Is £8 above or below what the market was paying?
steps.hint: £8 is more than the £6 workers were getting.

steps.q: At the old £6 wage, the quantity of labour supplied equalled the quantity demanded. If firms must now pay £8, do they want to hire the same number of workers as before?
steps.right: No, they want to hire fewer
steps.hint: Think of the labour demand curve: as the wage on the vertical axis rises, what happens to quantity demanded?
steps.pre: Firms cut back hiring while more people want jobs at £8, shown on a

steps.q: A government instead caps pay for a skilled job at £10, below the £14 the market was paying. At £10, do enough workers want these jobs to fill all the vacancies firms want to offer?
steps.right: No, fewer workers are willing to take them
steps.wrong: Yes, the same number as before
steps.hint: Lower pay on the wage axis moves you along the supply curve - which way?
steps.pre: Firms want more workers than are willing to work at that low wage, shown on a

steps.q: Paying £8 instead of £6 an hour for the same job raises what a firm must spend on each worker it keeps. What might a firm do to make up for this extra spending?
steps.right: Raise its prices or cut other benefits it offers staff
steps.wrong: Keep prices and benefits exactly the same
steps.hint: The wage bill has gone up - where else could that extra money come from?
